input.vignette:
A 33-year-old male construction worker is brought to the emergency department with acute confusion after being found unconscious at his worksite. His medical history includes seizure disorder and schizophrenia, for which he takes haloperidol. He underwent an appendectomy two months ago. On examination, his vital signs show: temperature 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure 120/84 mmHg, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The patient is confused and non-communicative, with sweat-soaked clothing. While he shows no clear focal neurologic deficits, he lacks purposeful movement of his extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Anticholinergic toxicity
B. Exertional heat stroke
C. Malignant hyperthermia
D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
E. Central nervous system infection
F. Drug-induced hyperthermia
G. Septic shock
H. Nonexertional heat stroke
I. Thyroid storm
J. Status epilepticus

knowledge_chunks.title: Malignant hyperthermia: a review. > Etiology
knowledge_chunks.text: Genetically susceptible patients can have a malignant hyperthermia reaction in response to triggering agents such as halogenated anesthetic gasses and/or succinylcholine and more rarely to stressors such as vigorous exercise and heat exposure. Nitrous Oxide and Xenon, although they are inhaled anesthetics, are not halogenated and have not been implicated in malignant hyperthermia.

knowledge_chunks.title: A Comprehensive Understanding of Psychomotor Agitation: From Causes to Hospital Care. > TREATMENT OF PMA > Psychiatric Emergency Settings
knowledge_chunks.text: In clinical practice, different psychoactive drugs are often administered together. The combination of haloperidol and lorazepam has been studied, highlighting a lower incidence of extrapyramidal effects than haloperidol alone, providing a more rapid reduction of agitation and resulting superior to the combination of haloperidol, lorazepam and diphenhydramine. As for SGAs, there is still no sufficient evidence supporting their combination with BDZs or their use in alcohol intoxication. According to the FDA, parenteral BDZs should not be administered with intramuscular olanzapine. This warning is in contrast with some of the available evidence and underlines the necessity of further investigations better to evaluate the safety profile of this treatment combination.

knowledge_chunks.title: Genetic causes of acute encephalopathy in adults: beyond inherited metabolic and epileptic disorders. > Methods > Vanishing white matter disease
knowledge_chunks.text: The disease affects predominantly infants and young children; however, adolescent and adult onset are remarkable in approximately 25% of all cases. A defining characteristic of VWM that facilitates its recognition from other leukodystrophies is the occurrence (even at the outset of the disease) of discrete episodes of neurological deterioration superimposed on a background of chronic progressive course. According to natural history data from multicenter, longitudinal studies, the episodes involve motor problems and cognitive disturbance, whereas in nearly 60% of cases they consist of confusion or coma. Typical provoking factors of these crises in descending order of frequency include febrile illness, minor head injury, subclinical infections, anesthesia, acute psychologic stress, hyperthermia, and seizures.

Clinical Features 
 Unsteady gait in all cases
 Postinfectious cerebellitis: 1-3 weeks post URI like illness or immunization, truncal ataxia and gait instability, normal mental status, normal vitals, ONLY ataxia

knowledge_chunks.title: Heat stroke. > Introduction
knowledge_chunks.text: Heat-related illness is a spectrum of conditions progressing from heat exhaustion and heat injury to life-threatening heat stroke. Heat stroke is a clinical constellation of symptoms that include a severe elevation in body temperature, typically, but not always, greater than 40°C. Also, there must be clinical signs of central nervous system dysfunction, including ataxia, delirium, or seizures, in the setting of exposure to hot weather or strenuous physical exertion.[1] Risk factors include environmental variables, medications, drug use, and other medical comorbidities.[2]

knowledge_chunks.title: The consolidation of neuroleptic therapy: Janssen, the discovery of haloperidol and its introduction into clinical practice. > Toxicity
knowledge_chunks.text: Toxicities are the exaggerated symptoms of known pharmacological effects and adverse drug reactions. The most prominent toxicities of haloperidol are severe extrapyramidal symptoms, hypotension, and sedation. The patient may appear comatose with severe respiratory depression or shock from hypotension. The extrapyramidal symptoms include akathisia, rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor, and acute dystonia. Haloperidol overdose can cause torsades de pointes, a type of ECG change that leads to arrhythmia or cardiac arrest.[24]
